name: Saint Petersburg
info: Saint Petersburg is a city on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland in Russia, founded by Peter the Great in 1703 and capital of the Russian Empire until 1918, later Petrograd and Leningrad.

facts.founded: On 27 May 1703 (16 May in the Julian calendar) by Tsar Peter the Great, who laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy (Hare) Island after capturing the Swedish fortress of Nyenskans.
facts.where: On the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland on the Baltic Sea, on the islands of the river's delta and the lowlands along Neva Bay, in north-western Russia.
facts.known: Peter the Great's founding on a captured Swedish site; capital of the Russian Empire; the Winter Palace and the Hermitage; the Decembrist revolt of 1825; the revolutions of 1905 and 1917; the siege of Leningrad of 1941 to 1944; its canals and bridges
facts.today: Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, after Moscow, and is governed as a federal city.

t: Peter the Great founded the city on 27 May 1703 on land taken from Sweden, using conscripted serfs, and moved the capital there in 1712.
It was the seat of the Russian court and government for most of the time until 1918, and the revolutions of 1905 and 1917 began there before the Bolsheviks moved the government to Moscow in 1918.
It was renamed Petrograd in 1914 and Leningrad in 1924, survived a siege of 872 days from 1941 to 1944, and took back the name Saint Petersburg in 1991.
dyk: In 1914 Tsar Nicholas II renamed the city Petrograd to remove the German words Sankt and Burg from its name. It became Leningrad in 1924, and a referendum in 1991 restored the name Saint Petersburg.

sections.origins:
Saint Petersburg stands on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland, on the islands of the river's delta and the lowlands beside Neva Bay. Before the 17th century the area was inhabited by Finnic Izhorians and Votians. Swedish colonists built the fortress of Nyenskans at the mouth of the Neva in 1611, and the small town of Nyen grew up around it. Ingrian Finns moved to the region from Karelia and Savonia during the Swedish rule, and there were also some Estonian, Karelian, Russian and German inhabitants.

At the end of the 17th century Peter the Great wanted a seaport from which Russia could trade with the rest of Europe. Arkhangelsk, the country's main port, lay on the White Sea in the far north and was closed to shipping in winter. On 12 May 1703 (1 May in the Julian calendar), during the Great Northern War, Peter captured Nyenskans. On 27 May 1703 he laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy (Hare) Island, closer to the estuary, and it became the first brick and stone building of the new city. He named the city after his patron saint, the apostle Peter.

The city was built under harsh conditions by conscripted serfs from all over Russia. Peter ordered a yearly conscription of 40,000 serfs, and tens of thousands of them died in the work. The marshland was drained under German and Dutch engineers whom Peter had invited to Russia.
sections.growth:
Peter moved the capital from Moscow to Saint Petersburg in 1712, nine years before the Treaty of Nystad ended the war, and he had called it the capital as early as 1704. The city became a seaport, a naval base protected by the fortress of Kronstadt, and what Russians called the "window to Europe". Peter restricted the building of stone houses in the rest of Russia so that stonemasons would come to the new city, and he hired engineers, architects, shipbuilders and merchants from across Europe. In 1716 Domenico Trezzini drew up a plan with the centre on Vasilyevsky Island and a rectangular grid of canals; it was not completed, but it shows in the layout of the streets. In 1724 the Academy of Sciences, the University and the Academic Gymnasium were founded.

After the fires of 1736 and 1737 a committee under Burkhard Christoph von Münnich commissioned a new plan, which moved the centre to the Admiralty borough and set three radial streets running from the Admiralty, among them Nevsky Prospect. Baroque building reached its height with Rastrelli's Winter Palace, and neoclassical architecture followed from the 1760s. Under Catherine the Great the banks of the Neva were lined with granite embankments.

After the emancipation of the serfs in 1861 and industrialisation, many former peasants came to the capital. The city passed Moscow in population and industrial growth, and its population stood at 2.4 million in 1916.
sections.rulers:
The site belonged to Sweden until Peter the Great took it in 1703, during the Great Northern War. Aleksandr Menshikov, Peter's close friend, was the first governor general of the Saint Petersburg Governorate from 1703 to 1727, and was arrested and exiled to Siberia after Peter's death in 1725. In 1728 Peter II moved the seat of government back to Moscow, but in 1732, under Empress Anna, Saint Petersburg became the capital again, and it remained the seat of the Romanov dynasty and the government until 1917.

Several rulers met violent ends in or near the city. Peter III was supposedly killed in 1762 in a conspiracy led by his wife, Catherine the Great, Paul I was assassinated in 1801 and Alexander II was killed by terrorists in 1881. In March 1917 Nicholas II abdicated, ending over three hundred years of Romanov rule, and on 7 November 1917 the Bolsheviks under Lenin stormed the Winter Palace. In March 1918 Lenin moved the Soviet government to Moscow, away from the border.

The city was renamed Petrograd in 1914 and Leningrad in 1924. In 1931 Leningrad was separated administratively from Leningrad Oblast. In 1991 Anatoly Sobchak became its first directly elected mayor, and the city again took the name Saint Petersburg. The Constitutional Court of Russia moved to Senate Square in 2008.
sections.life:
The educated immigrants whom Peter brought made the city more cosmopolitan than Moscow. The Kunstkamera, founded in 1714 to collect curiosities from all over the world, is sometimes considered the first museum in Russia. The Saint Petersburg Conservatory was founded in 1862 by Anton Rubinstein, and Tchaikovsky, Prokofiev and Shostakovich were among its alumni. Pushkin, Gogol, Dostoyevsky and other writers set works in the city, and Dostoyevsky called it "the most abstract and intentional city in the world". The Mariinsky Theatre became the home of a ballet company and opera, and dancers such as Nijinsky and Anna Pavlova were its principal stars.

The city was laid out around its water. Peter proposed boats as a means of transport in a city of canals, inspired by Venice and Amsterdam. At first only a few small bridges crossed the smaller waterways, and a pontoon bridge was built over the Neva each summer; the first permanent bridge over the Neva, the Annunciation Bridge, opened in 1850. Nevsky Prospect became the main street. Orthodox, Lutheran and Catholic churches stood along it, and the Saint Petersburg Mosque, the largest mosque in Europe when it opened in 1913, stood on the right bank.

In the Soviet period many large apartments were divided among several families in communal flats, and by the 1930s 68 per cent of the population lived in such housing, under very poor conditions.
sections.crises:
The city stood on low ground, and parts of it suffered repeated floods. The worst, in 1824, reached 4.21 metres above sea level and destroyed over 300 buildings. Fires in 1736 and 1737 were catastrophic. In 1825 the Decembrist revolt took place on Senate Square, a day after Nicholas I assumed the throne. The Revolution of 1905 began in the city. Between 1917 and the 1930s about two million people fled the city, and its population fell from 2.4 million in 1916 to under 740,000 by 1920. After Sergei Kirov was assassinated on 1 December 1934, the Great Purge followed, and approximately 40,000 people were executed in Leningrad in Stalin's purges. In the Leningrad affair of 1949 to 1952 the city's party leadership was destroyed, and 23 leaders were sentenced to death.

German forces besieged Leningrad from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944, 872 days. The city was shelled and bombed, and the only route for supplies was the Road of Life across Lake Ladoga, which could be used only once the lake froze. On 20 November 1941 the bread ration fell to 250 grams for a worker and 125 grams for others. More than one million civilians were killed, mainly from starvation, and some accounts give about 1.2 million of 3 million. About 2,000 residents were arrested for cannibalism. The city's population fell from 3 million in 1941 to under 600,000 by the end of 1943.
sections.legacy:
Leningrad was named a Hero City in 1945 in Stalin's order of 1 May, and a law of 1965 confirmed the title. It received the Order of Lenin and the Gold Star medal for the resistance of the city and the endurance of those who survived the siege. The city was rebuilt over the following decades, partly according to prewar plans, and the Amber Room, looted by the Germans from the Catherine Palace, was re-created in 2003.

The centre of Saint Petersburg, mostly Baroque and neoclassical buildings of the 18th and 19th centuries, has been largely preserved. Because the capital moved to Moscow, later large building projects tended to be put up there, which helped keep the old centre's appearance. Many historic churches and some other buildings were destroyed in the Soviet period for ideological reasons. Since 1991 the Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Hermitage, which includes the Winter Palace, is one of the largest art museums in the world, and the Bronze Horseman, the equestrian monument to Peter the Great on Senate Square, is among the city's best-known symbols.

Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city of Russia, with about 5.6 million people in the 2021 census. It is a federal city, and from 1991 it again bears the name given to it by Peter the Great.

summary: Saint Petersburg, on the Neva at the head of the Gulf of Finland, was founded by Peter the Great in 1703 and was the capital of the Russian Empire until 1918. It was renamed Petrograd and Leningrad, endured a siege of 872 days, and is now Russia's second-largest city.
notes: CONFLICTS between the two articles, resolved by leaving the point out or choosing the wording that fits both: the 1914 renaming date (31 August O.S. 18 August / 1 September), the 1924 renaming date (24 or 26 January), Lenin's move to Moscow (5 or 12 March 1918, so only 'March 1918'), the 1991 name change (6 September, or 1 October in the lead), the metro's opening stations (6, 7 or 8, left out), the capital's gap (c. 1728-1730 in the lead, 1728-1732 in the text; I used 1728 and 1732).

SIEGE DEATHS: the lead says 'more than one million civilians, mainly from starvation'; the history article says about 1.2 million of 3 million civilians. I give both, attributed as 'some accounts'. Population falling to under 600,000 is from the main article's demographics section.

LENINGRAD AFFAIR: the main article gives 23 death sentences and 181 prison or exile terms (rehabilitated 1954); the history article says 'hundreds executed' in the late 1940s and 1950s. I used only the 23.
Peter III 'supposedly killed' in a conspiracy led by Catherine: hedge kept as in the article. The Amber Room: the history article says the Germans took it; the 2003 re-creation is as given there.
The history article says the city had 'two million' leave between 1917 and the 1930s; the population figure 740,000 by 1920 is the main article's.

Left out: tourism, economy, industry, climate, sports, transport, the present government, the Lakhta Center, the controversy about the skyline and the 2018 tourist figures. Nicknames (Venice of the North, White Nights) left out; 'window to Europe' is kept.

The history article says the city was 'the fourth largest city in Europe' by 1900; I did not use it. The history article's statement that Moscow remained the capital 'ever since' 1918 is not stated either.
The referendum percentages differ between the articles (55 per cent for Saint Petersburg in the main article, 54 per cent in the history article), so no percentage is given.
